rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The segment treats faʿl adjectives such as ṣald under its adjective-plural rules, distinguishing them from noun patterns.
rows.anchor: وأما ما كان فعلا فإنه لم يكسر على ما كسر عليه اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿl adjectives normally take faʿāl rather than the small-number noun pattern, because they modify counted nouns instead of taking numbers directly.
rows.anchor: أما ما كان فعلا فإنه يكسر على فعال ولا يكسر على بناء أدنى العدد

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some faʿl adjectives also take fuʿūl; Arabs were heard saying fasl and fusūl, paralleling noun pluralization.
rows.anchor: العرب من يقول فسل وفسول فكسروه على فعول كما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human adjectives in this class can take the sound masculine plural, as in ṣaʿbūn and khadlūn.
rows.anchor: للآدميين يمتنع من أن تجمعه بالواو والنون وذلك قولك صعبون

rows.speaker: الراجز
rows.claim: A rajaz line ending in manātīn serves as poetic evidence that human adjectives can take the sound masculine plural.
rows.anchor: وقال ~~الراجز # % قالت سليمى لا أحب الجعد بن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adjectives with feminine tāʾ usually take faʿāl plurals; they may also take -āt, but the medial consonant stays unvowelled because the form is adjectival.
rows.anchor: إذا لحقته الهاء للتأنيث كسر على فعال وذلك عبلة وعبال

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: The plural shiyāh has a medial vowel because some Arabs say shāh lajbah, and the plural follows that form.
rows.anchor: وقالوا شياه فحركوا الحرف الأوسط لأن من العرب من يقول شاة لجبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ribʿah is a feminine noun used of men and women, explaining rijāl ribʿāt and niswah ribʿāt, like the feminine numeral khamsah applied to men.
rows.anchor: يقولون رجال ربعات ونسوة ربعات وذلك لأن أصل ربعة اسم مؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some faʿl adjectives have identical singular and plural forms, as with kathth, thaṭṭ, and jaww.
rows.anchor: فعل فقالوا رجل كث وقوم كث وقالوا ثط وثط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forms used as nouns may take ordinary noun plurals, including afʿul, ʿabīd, and ʿibād.
rows.anchor: استعمال الأسماء ~~على أفعل وذلك عبد وأعبد وقالوا عبيد وعباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Related forms admit several noun-like plurals: shaykh has ashāyikh or shaykhān, ḍayf has ḍayfān or ḍuyūf, and waghad has waghadān.
rows.anchor: والشيخ نحو من ذلك قالوا أشياخ كما قالوا أبيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿal adjectives commonly pluralize on fiʿāl, as in ḥasan/ḥisān, sabiṭ/sibāṭ, and qaṭaṭ/qiṭāṭ.
rows.anchor: يكسرونه على فعال كما كسروا الفعل واتفقا عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿal adjectives can instead take afʿāl, a pattern also used for faʿl, making it a substitute for fiʿāl.
rows.anchor: وربما كسروه على ~~أفعال لأنه مما يكسر عليه فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feminine forms in the faʿal class take fiʿāl when their masculine follows that pattern; human forms may also take sound masculine endings.
rows.anchor: الهاء للتأنيث كسر على فعال كما فعل ذلك بفعل وليس شيء من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Where the masculine takes afʿāl rather than fiʿāl, its feminine counterpart takes the sound feminine plural in -āt, as in baṭlah/baṭalāt.
rows.anchor: الهاء للتأنيث كسر على فعال كما فعل ذلك بفعل وليس شيء من هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣanʿ and rajul form sound masculine plurals without broken forms; faʿl is less common than faʿal as an adjective.
rows.anchor: وقالوا رجل صنع ~~وقوم صنعون ورجل رجل وقوم رجلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿl adjectives are rare; janub may be ajnاب or janbūn, while shalil only forms shallūn.
rows.anchor: جنب فمن جمع من العرب قال أجناب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿl adjectives may use afʿāl instead of fuʿūl or fiʿāl, as in jilf/ajlāf, naḍw/anḍāʾ, and naqḍ/anqāḍ; some say ajlaf.
rows.anchor: وأما ما كان فعلا فإنهم قد كسروه على أفعال فجعلوه بدلا من فعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human faʿl adjectives can take sound masculine endings; ʿilj and ʿiljalah behave like nouns, as shown by the noun plural aʿlāj.
rows.anchor: وقالوا رجل صنع وقوم صنعون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rare faʿl class includes ḥulw/ḥulwūn and murr/āmrar; its feminine forms take -āt, and faʿl shares afʿāl plurals with faʿl.
rows.anchor: يقولون رجل حلو وقوم حلوون ومؤنثه يجمع بالتاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective jadd, meaning great in fortune, takes only the sound masculine plural jaddūn; faʿl is rarer than faʿl among adjectives.
rows.anchor: جد للعظيم الجد فلا يجمعونه إلا بالواو والنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿl adjectives generally avoid noun-like broken plurals because the pattern is rare in nouns and sound masculine pluralization is available.
rows.anchor: وأما ما كان فعلا فإنه لم يكسر على ما كسر عليه اسما لقلته في الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faʿl adjectives may take afʿāl, as in najd/anjād and yaqẓ/ayqāẓ.
rows.anchor: قالوا نجد وأنجاد ويقظ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fazaʿ, faraq, and wajil take -ūn, while nakad takes ankād, analogized to nouns because it shares their pattern.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولهم قوم فزعون وقوم فرقون وقوم وجلون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alif inclines toward imāla when followed by kasra, drawing pronunciation toward yāʾ for ease.
rows.anchor: فالألف تمال إذا كان بعدها حرف مكسور وذلك قولك عابد وعالم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imāla is an articulatory approximation, like moving ṣād toward zāy in ṣadr to ease the tongue's movement.
rows.anchor: يقربوها منها كما قربوا في الإدغام الصاد من الزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A single intervening mobile consonant does not block imāla from an initial kasra, as in ʿimād.
rows.anchor: أول حرف من الكلمة وبين الألف حرف متحرك والأول مكسور نحو عماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In longer nouns from a wāw root, the final alif may incline toward yāʾ once the form has developed a yāʾ, the relevant pattern for musammā.
rows.anchor: فإذا بلغت الأسماء أربعة أحرف أو جاوزت من بنات الواو فالإمالة مستتبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two intervening consonants still permit imāla when the first is quiescent, since a sākin is a weak barrier.
rows.anchor: الساكن ليس بحاجز قوي وإنما يرفع لسانه عن الحرف المتحرك

rows.speaker: أهل الحجاز
rows.claim: Hijazis do not apply imāla to the described forms such as sirbāl, shamāl, ʿimād, and kilāb.
rows.anchor: وجميع هذا لا يميله أهل الحجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No imāla occurs when the following vowel is fatḥa or ḍamma: fatḥa is closer to alif, while rounding toward wāw would change the letter.
rows.anchor: فإذا كان ما بعد الألف مضموما أو مفتوحا لم تكن فيه إمالة وذلك نحو آجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A preceding fatḥa or ḍamma also prevents imāla, as in ribāb, jimād, and al-balbāl.
rows.anchor: وكذلك إذا كان الحرف الذي قبل الألف مفتوحا أو مضموما نحو رباب وجماد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some incline the alif of as-siwidād because widād behaves like kilāb, a form that accepts imāla.
rows.anchor: الفعال لأن ودادا بمنزلة كلاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In roots with underlying yāʾ, an open alif is inclined because it occupies the place of yāʾ or replaces it.
rows.anchor: فكذا نحوا نحو الياء

rows.speaker: الفرزدق
rows.claim: Al-Farazdaq's verse with yashumm supports the yāʾ-directed pronunciation used as evidence for imāla.
rows.anchor: وقال الفرزدق # % وما حل من جهل حبى حلمائنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In wāw roots, imāla follows because final wāw turns to yāʾ after three letters, whereas yāʾ does not turn to wāw; yāʾ is lighter.
rows.anchor: جاوزت ثلاثة أحرف قلبت ياء والياء لا تقلب على هذه الصفة واوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some preserve the wāw quality and avoid imāla in short three-letter wāw-root nouns such as qafā, ʿaṣā, and al-qaṭā.
rows.anchor: من بنات الواو نحو قفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verb alifs from wāw roots incline consistently because the final consonant changes toward yāʾ across inflection; nouns do not undergo that same change.
rows.anchor: إذا قلت غزا وصفا ودعا

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Many speakers, including many Tamimis, leave open the alif of four-or-more-letter nouns from wāw roots.
rows.anchor: وجميع هذا لا يميله ناس كثير من بني تميم وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An added final alif is often inclined because it behaves like the alif of a yāʾ-root.
rows.anchor: ومما يميلون ألفه كل اسم كانت في آخره ألف زائدة للتأنيث

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Many speakers leave the feminine or other added final alif open, saying ḥublā and maʿzā.
rows.anchor: يقولون حبلى ومعزى | ومما يميلون ألفه كل شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Hijazis incline alif in weak-root forms when the first vowel of faʿaltu is kasra; ordinary speakers do not.
rows.anchor: إذا كان أول فعلت مكسورا نحوا نحو الكسر

rows.speaker: ابن أبي إسحاق
rows.claim: Ibn Abī Isḥāq reportedly heard Kathīr ʿAzzah say ṣāra; some recited khāfa with imāla, illustrating the restricted middle-wāw case.
rows.anchor: وبلغنا عن ابن أبي إسحاق أنه سمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With medial wāw, imāla is limited to forms beginning with kasra; qāma and dāra do not incline.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك قام ودار لا يميلونهما

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some say māta while others say mittu; speakers who say ṣāra and khāfa also use this variation.
rows.anchor: وقالوا مات وهم الذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alif in kiyāl and bayyāʿ is inclined because a preceding yāʾ functions like a kasra; many Arabs leave it open.
rows.anchor: ومما تمال ألفه قولهم كيال وبياع

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Speakers who do not incline kiyāl also leave open shaybān, Qays ʿAylān, and Ghaylān, while others incline them for the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: لا يميلون في كيال لا يميلون ههنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In a genitive position, some incline alif as in bābihi and mālihi by analogy with kātib and sājid, but the imāla is weaker because the kasra is not fixed.
rows.anchor: هذا في موضع الجر وشبهوه بفاعل نحو كاتب وساجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some extend imāla to accusative zaydan by analogy with Ghaylān, but it is weaker; they do not incline ʿabdan or kaslān because those lack yāʾ.
rows.anchor: كما فعلوا ذلك بغيلان

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some incline qazḥan and ʿalaman by treating their kasra as though it were yāʾ, and use the same analogy for al-najjādain.
rows.anchor: جعلوا الكسرة كالياء وقالوا في النجادين

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: In genitive forms such as ʿajlānik and mālin kathīr, speakers incline by analogy with bābik and with māshin and dāʿin.
rows.anchor: وقالوا في الجر مررت بعجلانك فأمالوا كما قالوا مررت ببابك

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Speakers differ at pause: some keep imāla, while others open the alif because pausing removes the supporting kasra.
rows.anchor: ومنهم من ينصب في الوقف

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some incline ʿimādan by analogy with imāla after kasra, while others keep ʿalaman and ʿimādan open without preceding yāʾ or kasra.
rows.anchor: وقال ناس رأيت عمادا فأمالوا للإمالة كما

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some pause with bimālin min ʿindi llāh or li-Zaydin māl, analogizing to ʿimād; this is weaker than a connected kasra.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض الذين يقولون في السكت بمال من عند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They do not say dhā māl this way because a medial alif resembles that of fāʿil; in ʿimādan the second alif follows the first in imāla.
rows.anchor: لم ~~يقولوا ذا مال يريدون ذا التي في هذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second alif in ʿimādan is inclined by the imāla of the first.
rows.anchor: وتقول عمادا تميل الألف الثانية لإمالة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An annexed noun used as a vocative is accusative by an unspoken verb; the singular vocative is nominative in form but occupies an accusative position.
rows.anchor: اعلم أن النداء كل اسم مضاف فيه فهو نصب

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says annexed vocatives and long indefinite calls such as ya rajulan ṣāliḥan are accusative.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه الله أنهم ~~نصبوا المضاف نحو يا عبد الله ويا اخانا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A standalone singular vocative is raised like qablu and baʿdu, though it occupies an accusative position.
rows.anchor: وذلك لأنه كثر في كلامهم فحذفوه

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl allows ya Zayd al-ṭawīlu to be accusative as an adjective of an accusative or as an understood aʿnī, “I mean.”
rows.anchor: قال نصب لأنه صفة لمنصوب

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl also allows the adjective to be nominative as an adjective of the raised vocative.
rows.anchor: من قبل أن كل اسم مفرد في النداء مرفوع أبدا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains the nominative adjective by the consistent nominative marking of every isolated vocative, unlike nouns in amsi al-aḥdathu.
rows.anchor: من قبل أن كل اسم مفرد في النداء مرفوع أبدا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: An adjective that is itself annexed follows the accusative of its vocative; raising it as a standalone vocative would be ungrammatical.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه الله أنهم ~~نصبوا المضاف نحو يا عبد الله ويا اخانا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says ya Zayd nafsahu, ya Tamīm kullakum, and ya Qays kullahum are accusative, like ya Zayd dhā al-jummati.
rows.anchor: يا تميم أجمعون فأنت فيه بالخيار إن شئت

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: With ya Tamīm ajmaʿūn, either nominative or accusative is possible; accusative cannot be an aʿnī construction.
rows.anchor: يا تميم أجمعون فأنت فيه بالخيار إن شئت

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus says the meaning is the same in the nominative and accusative, supporting the accusative adjective analysis.
rows.anchor: ويدلك على أن أجمعين ينتصب لأنه وصف لمنصوب قول يونس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An annexed adjective of a vocative should be accusative whenever the corresponding singular adjective is accusative.
rows.anchor: إذا كان المفرد بنتصب في الصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ya akhānā Zaydan is coordinated with the preceding accusative; Yūnus reports Abu ʿAmr and Medina speakers also say ya akhānā Zayd.
rows.anchor: وقال قوم يا أخانا زيد

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that Abū ʿAmr and the people of Medina say ya akhānā Zayd, treating the adjective like a standalone vocative.
rows.anchor: وتقول يا زيد زيد الطويل وهو قول أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ya akhānā Zaydan is more common because speakers restore the original accusative after the name leaves the vocative position.
rows.anchor: فأما المفرد إذا كان منادى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A standalone singular vocative is raised without tanwīn because frequent use led speakers to shorten it and treat it like an interjection.
rows.anchor: بغير تنوين وذلك لأنه كثر في كلامهم

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr says ya Zayd Zayd al-ṭawīlu, repeating the name in a construction explained like ya Zayd al-ṭawīlu.
rows.anchor: وتقول يا زيد زيد الطويل وهو قول أبي عمرو

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that Ruʾbah used the accusative repetition ya Zayd Zaydan al-ṭawīlu.
rows.anchor: وزعم يونس أن رؤبة كان يقول يا زيد زيدا الطويل

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾbah's verse ya Naṣru Naṣran Naṣran supports the accusative appositional repetition; Abū ʿAmr's form restarts the vocative.
rows.anchor: وقال رؤبة # % إني وأسطار سطرن سطرا % % لقائل يا نصر نصرا نصرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adjective of a standalone vocative differs from that of amsi because nominative marking is consistent across vocatives.
rows.anchor: وبعضهم ينشد # % يا نصر نصر نصرا

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Some recite ya Naṣru Naṣru Naṣran, retaining a raised second name before the final accusative form.
rows.anchor: ينشد # % يا نصر نصر نصرا % %

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coordination such as ya Zayd wa-ʿAmr shares the vocative particle across names; the second name is not an adjective.
rows.anchor: يا زيد وعمرو ليس إلا لأنهما قد اشتركا

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl explains accusative al-Naḍr in ya Zayd wa-l-Naḍra as restoration to the underlying case.
rows.anchor: الخليل رحمه الله من قال يا زيد والنضر فنصب

rows.speaker: العرب
rows.claim: Most Arabs whom Sībawayh observed say ya Zayd wa-l-Naḍru with the second name raised.
rows.anchor: ما رأيناهم يقولون يا زيد والنضر

rows.speaker: الأعرج
rows.claim: Al-Aʿraj recited wa-l-ṭayru in the nominative, illustrating coordination within the vocative construction.
rows.anchor: يا جبال أوبي معه والطير

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl treats ya ʿAmru wa-l-Ḥārith as though ya were repeated; a definite noun with alif-lām cannot itself be directly called by ya.
rows.anchor: هو القياس كأنه قال ويا حارث

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl argues that accusative al-Naḍr would wrongly license accusative sakhlihā in kullu naʿjatin wa-sakhlihā, though its case comes from an understood preposition.
rows.anchor: ينبغي لمن قال النضر فنصب لأنه لا يجوز يا النضر

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl says raising the coordinated definite noun treats it as wa-Nuḍr; conjunctions share the first element's syntactic governance.
rows.anchor: أي فتى هيجاء أنت وجارها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A coordinated element that follows later enters the same syntactic relation as the first; direct adjacency can prevent the intended indefinite reading.
rows.anchor: لو قلت ~~هذا فصيلها لم يكن نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's ya ayyuhā address follows the construction illustrated by ya ayyuha al-rajulu; a coordinated name remains carried by ya.
rows.anchor: قال رؤبة # % يا دار عفراء ودار البخدن

rows.speaker: رؤبة
rows.claim: Ruʾbah's ya dāra ʿAfrāʾ wa-dāra al-bakhdani is poetic evidence that a coordinated phrase remains carried by ya.
rows.anchor: رؤبة # % يا دار عفراء ودار البخدن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ya hādhā dhā al-jummati has the same construction as ya Zayd dhā al-jummati, with no disagreement.
rows.anchor: وتقول يا هذا ذا الجمة كقولك يا زيد ذا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from ʿAdī, Ghanī, Quṣayy, and Umayyah uses wāw to avoid four consecutive yāʾs, deleting the extra yāʾ as in Sulaym and Thaqīf.
rows.anchor: وذلك قولك في عدي عدوي وفي غني غنوي وفي قصي قصوي وفي أمية أموي

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports that some Arabs retain the yāʾ in Umayyī, analogizing to Ṭayyiʾī; ʿAdiyyī is heavier because of the kasra among yāʾs.
rows.anchor: وزعم يونس أن ناسا من العرب يقولون أميي فلا يغيرون لما صار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from ḥayyah becomes ḥayawī to avoid consecutive yāʾs; the yāʾ is vocalized so wāw can remain after it.
rows.anchor: فقال حيوي كراهية أن تجتمع الياءات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tribal name Ḥayy ibn Bahdalah supplies evidence for ḥayawī and for vocalizing yāʾ before wāw.
rows.anchor: حركت الياء لأنه لا تكون الواو ثابتة وقبلها ياء ساكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from layyah becomes lawawī by restoring the underlying form after moving yāʾ; speakers who say Umayyī also say ḥayyī.
rows.anchor: احتجت إلى أن تحرك هذه الياء كما احتجت

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abū ʿAmr used ḥayyī and layyī, including layyah from the phrase for twisting someone's hand.
rows.anchor: وكان أبو عمرو يقول حيي وليي ولية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from ʿaduww and kuwwah remains ʿaduwwī and kuwwī because there are not enough consecutive yāʾs to require substitution.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن الإضافة إلى عدو فقال عدوي وإلى كوة فقال كوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Marmawī is analogized to bakhtī because its ending has the same sequence of yāʾs and kasra; maghzawī keeps its form when no cluster arises.
rows.anchor: في الإضافة إلى مرمي فجعله بمنزلة البختي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from ʿadwah becomes ʿadawī because the feminine tāʾ triggers the same treatment as in shanrah/shanʾī.
rows.anchor: إلى عدوة قلت عدوي من أجل الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nisba from taḥiyyah becomes taḥwī, deleting the yāʾ most like the deleted element in ʿAdī; similar forms follow it.
rows.anchor: وسألته عن الإضافة إلى تحية فقال تحوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qusī and thudī yield qaswī and thadwī because they are fuʿūl forms; when the following kasra disappears, the original pattern returns.
rows.anchor: في الإضافة إلى قسي وثدي ثدوي وقسوي لأنها فعول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With marma and marmawwiyyah, delete the first two yāʾs and keep the nisba yāʾs; those saying ḥānawī also say marmwī.
rows.anchor: تحذف الياءين وتثبت ياءي الإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu resembles source-like nouns without matching them in every respect, functioning like wāḥidan fa-wāḥidan or rajulan rajulan.
rows.anchor: وهو قولك دخلوا الأول فالأول جرى على قولك واحدا فواحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'anic al-nāṣiyati nāṣiyatin kādhibatin supplies an example of an accusative noun followed by an appositional clarification.
rows.anchor: كما قال عز وجل @QB@ بالناصية ناصية كاذبة @QE@

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an imperative, accusative al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu is standard; it cannot be a badal or adjective because the corresponding readings are invalid.
rows.anchor: ولا يكون بدلا لأنك لو قلت ادخل الأول فالأول

rows.speaker: عيسى
rows.claim: ʿĪsā explains the imperative as meaning li-yadkhul, “let the first enter,” and parses the phrase according to that underlying meaning.
rows.anchor: وكان عيسى يقول ادخلوا الأول فالأول لأن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding wa-l-ṣaghīru wa-l-kabīru permits nominative because the phrase means “all of them.”
rows.anchor: فالرفع لأن معناه معنى كلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the words are intended as direct adjectives, fa cannot join them; wa is acceptable, as supported by Umayyah ibn Abī ʿĀʾidh's verse.
rows.anchor: مررت بزيد أخيك وصاحبك كان حسنا

rows.speaker: أمية بن أبي عائذ
rows.claim: Umayyah's poem with wa-shaʿthin supports coordination by wa; substituting fa before shaʿthin would be poor usage.
rows.anchor: والبيت لأميه بن أبى عائذ # % ويأوى إلى نسوة عطل

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl allows al-awwalu fa-l-awwalu wa-l-awsaṭu wa-l-ākhiru by treating the sequence as a badal construction like kullukum.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل ادخلوا الأول فالأول والأوسط والآخر
